blocks.text: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), formerly known as acute renal failure, is an abrupt reduction in kidney function occurring over hours to days, characterised by:

items.text: A rise in serum creatinine.
A reduction in urine output.
Impaired excretion of metabolic waste products.
Disturbances in fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance.

blocks.text: AKI may be reversible, particularly when the underlying cause is identified and treated promptly.

blocks.title: AKI is diagnosed when **any one** of the following is present:

items.text: Increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL (≥26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours.
Increase in serum creatinine to ≥1.5 times baseline, known or presumed to have occurred within the preceding 7 days.
Urine output less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 6 hours.

blocks.text: **Important:** A patient can have AKI based on urine output criteria even before serum creatinine rises significantly.

| Stage | Serum creatinine | Urine output |

| 1 | 1.5–1.9 times baseline OR increase ≥0.3 mg/dL |
Fluid overload may occur because of reduced urinary excretion, excessive fluid administration or both.

items.text: Restrict fluid intake.
Restrict sodium intake where appropriate.
Stop unnecessary IV fluids.
Use loop diuretics if clinically significant fluid overload is present and the patient is likely to respond.
Consider dialysis if fluid overload is severe or refractory.

blocks.text: **Prescription 3: Furosemide (adult)**
**Furosemide injection 20 mg/2 mL**

items.text: Dose: 20–40 mg.
Route: Intravenous.
Frequency: Once; repeat or titrate according to response and specialist advice.
Duration: Individualised.
Quantity: 1–2 ampoules, depending on the prescribed dose.
Administer slowly IV.
For IV doses up to 80 mg, do not exceed 4 mg/minute.
Monitor blood pressure, urine output, electrolytes and fluid balance.

blocks.text: In patients already receiving loop diuretics, a higher dose may be necessary because of reduced renal responsiveness.
**Important distinction:**
Furosemide does not reverse intrinsic kidney damage and has not been demonstrated to improve renal recovery or reduce mortality in AKI.
Its role is limited to management of fluid overload or oedema in selected patients.
Do not use it routinely to convert oliguric AKI into non-oliguric AKI.
**Prescription 4: Furosemide (paediatric)**

items.text: Dose: 0.5–1 mg/kg IV initially.
Frequency: Once; subsequent doses based on response and specialist advice.
Maximum: Follow paediatric renal and institutional protocols.
Administration: Give slowly IV, monitoring blood pressure, electrolytes and urine output.

blocks.text: For children with established AKI, diuretics should only be used when there is an appropriate indication, particularly clinically significant fluid overload.
Hyperkalaemia is one of the most dangerous complications of AKI because it can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

blocks.title: Management is covered comprehensively in Chapter 38. The immediate treatment principles are:

items.text: IV calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilisation when indicated.
IV insulin with glucose to shift potassium intracellularly.
Nebulised salbutamol as an adjunct.
Sodium bicarbonate in selected patients with significant metabolic acidosis.
Potassium removal through renal excretion, gastrointestinal binders or dialysis, depending on the circumstances.

blocks.text: **Important:** Calcium gluconate protects the myocardium but does not lower serum potassium.
Persistent or severe hyperkalaemia despite medical treatment requires urgent consideration of dialysis.
AKI may cause metabolic acidosis due to impaired renal acid excretion and reduced bicarbonate regeneration.

items.text: Treat the underlying cause.
Correct hypovolaemia where present.
Treat sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion.
Correct associated hyperkalaemia.
Consider sodium bicarbonate in selected patients with severe metabolic acidosis.
Consider renal replacement therapy if acidosis is severe and refractory.

items.text: Furosemide: Use cautiously where electrolyte depletion may precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
Sodium bicarbonate: Avoid unnecessary sodium loading.

blocks.text: Signs of improvement

items.text: Increasing urine output.
Falling serum creatinine.
Improving serum urea.
Normalisation of potassium.
Correction of metabolic acidosis.

Recovery of estimated kidney function as renal function stabilises.

blocks.text: **Important:** Serum creatinine may take time to fall after the underlying cause has been corrected. An immediate reduction in creatinine is not required to demonstrate an appropriate treatment response.

blocks.text: **1. Intermittent haemodialysis (IHD)**
Commonly used in haemodynamically stable patients. It removes excess fluid, electrolytes and uraemic toxins over several hours.
**2. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT)**
Particularly useful in haemodynamically unstable critically ill patients requiring gradual fluid and solute removal.
**3. Peritoneal dialysis (PD)**
Uses the peritoneal membrane for fluid and solute exchange. It is useful in selected patients, including children and neonates.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Discharge counselling, follow-up and high-yield clinical pearls

blocks.title: A patient recovering from AKI may be considered for discharge when:

items.text: The underlying cause has been addressed or is adequately controlled.
Haemodynamic status is stable.
Fluid balance can be maintained safely.
Electrolyte abnormalities are controlled.
There is no immediate indication for dialysis.
Renal function is stable or improving sufficiently for outpatient management.
A clear medication and follow-up plan is available.

blocks.text: Complete normalisation of creatinine is not always necessary before discharge.
There is no universal discharge prescription for AKI. Prescribe according to the underlying condition and residual kidney impairment.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. High-yield clinical pearls and examination points

blocks.text: **Remember these 15 points**

items.text: AKI is defined by KDIGO using serum creatinine and/or urine output.
The three KDIGO stages determine severity.
Pre-renal AKI results from reduced renal perfusion.
Intrinsic AKI results from damage to renal tissue.
Post-renal AKI results from urinary tract obstruction.
Acute tubular necrosis is a common cause of intrinsic AKI.
Hyperkalaemia is a potentially fatal complication.
Fluid replacement is indicated in hypovolaemic AKI, not indiscriminately in all AKI.
Furosemide does not improve renal recovery.
Low-dose dopamine is not recommended.
NSAIDs can precipitate or worsen AKI.
Urinary obstruction requires prompt decompression.
Persistent hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema and uraemic complications may require dialysis.
Creatinine and urine output should both be monitored.
Follow-up at approximately 3 months is important to identify persistent kidney disease.
